Sources indicate that A right-angle drill solves problems when a standard drill can’t reach—navigating between studs, working inside cabinets, or tackling tight corners. While this makes these specialized power tools handy in these situations, who truly needs a right-angle drill?

Sources indicate that plumbers, electricians, carpenters, and pretty much anyone involved in construction and renovation projects will appreciate having one handy. Even hobbyists and homeowners may need a right-angle drill when tackling certain jobs, such as installing cabinetry or assembling furniture.

We test the top right-angle drills to find the best models for pros and homeowners. Our favorite was the Ridgid thanks to its comprehensive kit, durable build, and impressive power. Below, find the results of our hands-on tests and learn how these models earned their spot in this lineup of the best right-angle drills.

Any of the following right-angle drills will make it easier to drill holes and drive screws in tight areas, but each one comes with some pros and cons. We’ve detailed both the benefits and the downsides noted during our tests. Some models are best suited to light-duty use, while others are powerhouses designed with construction pros in mind. There’s sure to be one that will suit your project needs.

Ridgid’s cordless right-angle drill manages to be compact and lightweight while still offering  tremendous drilling and driving power.

In a recent development, its head measures just 3.5 inches long, making it one of the shortest 18V or 20V angle drills we tested. Couple that with its slim profile and short length, and it fits easily into tight spaces inside cabinets and under-sink vanities.

Right-angle drills tend to be top-heavy, which can make them awkward to hold. With its compact size and light weight, the Ridgid was an exception. It felt comfortable and well balanced in the hand, which is significant given that these tools are often used in tight spaces where it’s not possible to get a two-handed grip. Adding to its maneuverability is a long trigger that’s easy to access from various hand positions. The trigger has ample rubberized grip, making it easy to keep a firm hold on the tool.

Given its smaller size, we expected it to come up lacking in power. It didn’t. With a max speed of 1,900 RPM, the Ridgid had no trouble handling the larger bits we tested, easily boring holes with a 1/2-inch twist bit and 1-inch spade bit. It followed up that impressive performance by effortlessly driving ten 3-inch carpenter screws into a couple of stacked 2x4s. And if you need additional torque, you can get its max 375 in-lbs (inch-pounds) by dropping down to its lower speed setting.

Industry observers note that what our tester claims: “Ridgid’s right-angle drill is everything you want out of this kind of specialty power tool. It’s compact and lightweight while still packing plenty of power for drilling large holes and driving fasteners.”—Tony Carrick, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the Ridgid right-angle drill at The Home Depot.

Ryobi’s tools have steadily grown more powerful over the years, slowly closing the gap with premium brands, and the PSBRA02 right-angled drill is a great example of the brand’s progression. With a max speed of 1,700 RPM and 350 in-lbs of torque, it can handle just about any job that requires this type of tool. Those specs also put it in the same ballpark as other cordless drills, all at a friendlier price point for DIYers who may not need premium performance.

According to recent reports, it produced enough power for drilling ½-inch holes with a twist bit and 1-inch holes with a paddle bit. It also didn’t struggle to drive a 3-inch carpentry screw through two 2x4s. The PSBRA02 won’t win any speed tests, but unless you’re drilling dozens of holes or driving loads of screws, you likely won’t notice the time difference.

The PSBRA02 isn’t the most compact right-angle drill out there, nor is it the largest. Nonetheless, it fits into compact spaces thanks to a head that measures just 3.5 inches long. It also feels comfortable in the hand with a manageable weight, plenty of rubberized grip around the handle, and a long trigger accessible from various hand positions.

Get the Ryobi right-angle drill at Amazon or The Home Depot.

Sources indicate that looking for a 12-volt right-angle drill that delivers impressive power? The Milwaukee cordless drill caught our attention for all the right reasons. We tested the kit version of this small right-angle drill, complete with a battery and charger. However, owners who already own 12V Milwaukee tools can order the drill as a “tool only” and utilize existing batteries.

This drill sits on the smaller side of the spectrum, weighing in at a mere 2.03 pounds. It slipped effortlessly into tight spots during tests, and its lightweight design let us comfortably operate it with just one hand. Since this drill packs less power than some other models we tested, it isn’t well-suited for heavy construction work. Instead, it excels at light-duty tasks like furniture assembly and drilling small holes in confined spaces. The integrated LED light was handy, though we did use an additional work light in darker areas.

Sources indicate that the real surprise here is the inclusion of a clutch, an essential feature that prevents stripping screw heads. What’s more, the elongated trigger design allowed us to adjust our grip up or down on the tool handle (based on comfort level) and still easily pull the trigger. While this drill is not intended for heavy-duty tasks, it’s a good choice for electricians, HVAC technicians, and plumbers who require precise screw insertion or minor hole drilling in tight spaces.

Get the Milwaukee right-angle drill at Amazon (tool only), Ace Hardware (tool only), or The Home Depot (battery included).

Industry observers note that look no further than the Bosch 12V Flexiclick drill. This handy tool boasts high and low speeds alongside a variable-speed trigger, and it performed admirably in our hands-on tests.

It has been revealed that unlike other 12V models, the Bosch Flexiclick isn’t confined solely to right-angle drilling. The array of attachments sets this drill apart, transforming it into a standard, offset, or right-angle drill by simply connecting the corresponding attachment.

Industry observers note that one of our favorite features was the head’s ability to rotate in any direction. This allowed us to insert fasteners at any angle, though it required two hands when using the rotating head. Weighing only 1.2 pounds, this drill is comfortable for extended use, yet it offers an impressive 1,750 RPM—a remarkable feat for a 12-volt model. A magnetic bit holder adds convenience and also prevents the frustration of dropped screws.

In a recent development, for DIY enthusiasts and shoppers seeking versatility without the need for heavy torque, the Bosch Flexiclick is a game changer. We found it effortless to change attachments thanks to the one-click interface, and it offers the ability to use the drill in multiple ways. A convenient storage case keeps everything organized.

Get the Bosch right-angle drill at Amazon, Lowe’s, or Acme Tools.

In a recent development, introducing the powerhouse of right-angle drills: The Makita DA4031. This electric drill stands out as a true performer. While it’s the only corded right-angle drill we tested, a host of impressive features make it an outstanding choice for construction pros.

This heavy-duty drill features a potent 10-amp motor that provided unwavering power in our tests, drilling effortlessly through wall studs and joists. We found the second-hand handle indispensable for robust drilling tasks, as it let us grip it firmly while drilling for additional support. Perhaps best of all, both our right- and left-handed testers were able to use the drill comfortably, thanks to the ability to attach the handle to either side of the tool.

The corded Makita made quick work of drilling large holes through ply materials and dimensional lumber. Its built-in clutch exhibited impeccable performance, effectively halting torque at low speeds when the tool met heavy resistance. With a drill this powerful, a good clutch is a must—not just to avoid stripping screw heads, but to keep you from breaking a wrist.

In a recent development, while the corded design offers a consistent power supply sans battery charging, it has limitations. Since we’re so used to cordless tools, we really noticed the Makita’s cord limitations, like having to drag a cord around and being limited to working near an electrical outlet.

For those seeking the ultimate right-angle drilling companion on the jobsite, it’s tough to beat the Makita DA4031 for its heavy-duty construction, durability, and reliable performance.

Get the Makita DA4031 right-angle drill at Amazon or Acme Tools.

DeWalt’s 20V MAX right-angle cordless drill packs plenty of power, though this brawn comes at the cost of its maneuverability in confined spaces. Still, the DCD740 blazed through our drilling tests. With its high speed and torque output, it bored a clean hole with a ½-inch twist bit and chipped out a surprisingly smooth 1-inch hole with a paddle bit. It was also a fast driver, sinking 3-inch carpentry screws faster than other cordless right-angle drills we tested.

Sources indicate that the DeWalt DCD740 has two speeds, so you can drop the speed down to max out the torque, which will help prevent stripping out screw heads. Along with its power output, the DCD740 also has a tougher feel than other right-angle drills with a metal chuck and thicker plastic housing.

It has been revealed that the DCD740 is one of the brand’s earliest 20V cordless tools. It uses a brushed motor and is larger and heavier than other right-angle drills. Its bare tool weight of just over 3 pounds may not sound like a lot, but it makes a difference when extending your arm to drive in a screw in the deeper recesses of a cabinet. Its larger body and longer head mean it won’t fit into as tight a space as other more compact models. Still, it’s a powerful right-angle drill and a great option for anyone who already owns a few DeWalt 20V cordless tools.

What our tester notes: “This may be one of DeWalt’s oldest cordless tools, but it packs more driving and drilling power than other cordless right-angle drills we tested.”—Tony Carrick, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the DeWalt DCD 740 at Lowe’s.

DeWalt’s handy right-angle attachment offers a creative solution for those who occasionally need access to confined spaces without buying a dedicated right-angle drill.

This ingenious accessory is not a stand-alone tool but a versatile addition that easily connects to the chuck of a ¼-inch standard DeWalt drill/driver or impact driver. It is well suited to even the tightest of spots and offers a convenient means of right-angle drilling and driving. As staunch admirers of DeWalt’s innovation and craftsmanship, we think this compact attachment lives up to the manufacturer’s stellar reputation.

Before testing the tools in this lineup, we researched more than 20 of the most popular right-angle drills and right-angle drill attachments. Our testing involved a range of tasks commonly encountered by professionals and DIY enthusiasts alike. We tested the drills’ capabilities in drilling holes through various materials, including studs and joists, to simulate the challenges faced during electrical and plumbing work. We also assessed their effectiveness for driving screws in tight spaces, such as cabinet bases and other confined areas.

Sources indicate that throughout our testing, we paid close attention to the drills’ power, precision, and ease of use. We tested the drills with different types of bits—including standard, auger, hole-saw, and driver bits—to assess their versatility across various applications. We evaluated their power and performance to gauge their ability to handle different tasks efficiently. We also looked for ergonomic design and user-friendliness, considering factors like grip comfort and the convenience of features like LED lights and soft start-ups.

Finally, we awarded points based on a rubric: The better a tool performed a task, the more points it received. After testing, we averaged the points to help determine the best uses for the different tools.

According to recent reports, the width of the head is perhaps the most crucial feature of a right-angle drill because it determines the space into which it can fit. However, there are several other key factors to take into account, including motor speed, power source, and weight. Ahead, learn more about these and other crucial attributes to think about when choosing the best right-angle drill.

It has been revealed that right-angle drills come in corded and cordless varieties, each with its own pros and cons. Cordless drills run on a rechargeable lithium-ion battery and offer the convenience and flexibility of not needing an electrical outlet or a cord. This lets you use them virtually anywhere.

In a recent development, corded models, in comparison, require a standard electrical outlet. While these drills aren’t as convenient, a 120V power supply makes them more powerful while providing a reliable and constant power supply. Corded drills are also generally less expensive than cordless models. As with many power tools, spending more on a cordless model makes sense if it will see regular use. A less expensive corded model should suffice for DIYers who may use a right-angle drill only occasionally.

Size and weight determine a right-angle drill’s functionality and ease of use. Because a right-angle drill is meant to fit into tight spaces, size is crucial. Most right-angle drills have a head between 3 and 4 inches wide, so they can reach places standard corded and cordless power drills can’t.

Right-angle drills can also be short and lightweight enough to manage with one hand—although heavy-duty models typically come with a secondary handle.

Chuck size is also vital. Most right-angle drills have a ⅜-inch chuck, which helps keep the head compact. Some larger models feature a ½-inch chuck for drilling larger holes or driving in bigger screws. These models typically have a wider head.

Right-angle drills have ergonomically shaped handles with rubberized grips that let you hold them securely with one hand while drilling. Many also have detachable side handles that let you apply more leverage with the other hand. Some manufacturers equip right-angle drills with paddle-style triggers that run the length of the handle. This feature lets you better regulate trigger pressure to control the drill’s speed.

In a recent development, A drill’s speed determines how quickly the tool can drill holes or drive screws. It also gives an indication of how much torque the drill produces if the manufacturer does not provide that information. Speed is measured in RPM and, in most cases, is directly related to the power source. Most cordless 18V right-angle drills top out at around 1,500 RPM, while some 20V drills can reach about 2,000 RPM.

Corded right-angle drills have access to more power, which means they can produce more RPM. A corded 4-amp right-angle drill boasts around 2,400 RPM. While speed isn’t the same as torque, motors that can produce higher RPM are more powerful and thus capable of producing more torque.

When assessing a cordless tool’s battery life, consider not only how long each charge lasts but also how long the battery itself will hold a charge before it needs replacing. Most batteries for right-angle cordless drills will last about 3 hours on a single charge with intermittent use and will take about 3 hours to recharge.

It has been revealed that lithium-ion batteries typically last about 3 years, or about 300 to 500 charging cycles, before they begin to lose their ability to hold a charge. This doesn’t mean the battery will stop working altogether. As a battery nears the end of its life, it will simply last for a shorter period of time and require more frequent charging.

It has been revealed that as with standard drills, right-angle drills are capable of using various types of bits and attachments. These drills are adept at drilling holes with standard drill bits or driving in screws with Phillips-head, flat, star, and other styles of screw-driving bits. These drills can also use socket attachments to drive bolts. Like other power tools, right-angle drills use a variety of accessories, including drill bits, screwdriver bits, chuck keys, and other accessories that can be misplaced. For this reason, many right-angle drills include a storage bag that holds the tool, accessories, batteries, and chargers all in one place for easy storage and transport.

Right-angle drills also often offer convenient features like LED lights that illuminate the work area and switches that make it easier to control the drill speed, permitting the user to increase or decrease the speed range to maximize control and improve torque.

For more information on how and where to best use a right-angle drill, read on for answers to some common questions about these power tools.

A right-angle drill has a geared head that rotates the chuck 90 degrees from the body’s axis, letting it reach tight spaces and drill or drive at angles a conventional drill can’t.

This versatile tool is helpful for a wide range of projects. It can be invaluable for fitting into tight spaces when working on a vehicle. A right-angle drill is also ideal for drilling between floor joists or wall studs, which are spaces that are typically too narrow for a standard drill.

A ⅜-inch drill has a chuck that can accommodate drill bits up to ⅜ inch. Similarly, a ½-inch drill has a larger chuck that can handle drill bits with a maximum diameter of ½ inch. A ½-inch drill generally offers more power and torque, making it suitable for drilling larger holes and tackling tougher materials. It’s commonly used in construction and heavy-duty applications.

A right-angle drill attachment is an accessory that can be added to a standard drill or driver to enable drilling and driving in tight or confined spaces that are difficult to access with a regular tool.

Yes. A right-angle drill can handle drilling tasks that require high torque and speed, depending on the type of drill. A model drill such as the Makita DA4031 or DeWalt DCD740 can drill large holes through floor joists, wall studs, and framing plates with ease.

In a recent development, most cordless drills don’t require you to do a lot to maintain them, but there are few things you can do to keep them in tip-top shape. Wipe off any sawdust or debris after each use, paying close attention to the chuck and air vents. Remove the battery when the drill isn’t in use and store it in a cool place. Lubricate the chuck periodically by applying a small amount of machine oil to the chuck jaws to prevent stiffness.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest danger with a right-angle drill is sudden kickback that can cause wrist injuries. If possible use two hands when operating a right-angle drill, one to control the trigger and the other on the back of the head to stabilize its motion. If that isn’t possible, brace the drill body or your arm against a solid object, like a wall stud, to prevent the tool from spinning out if it jams.

Bad Habits That Are Making Your Wood Deck Rot

  • A wooden deck adds charm to a backyard and serves as the ultimate backdrop for outdoor relaxation, but keeping it in prime condition requires some work.
  • Industry observers note that one of the biggest mistakes homeowners make when it comes to wooden deck care is pressure-washing it too aggressively, which often strips the wood fibers, splinters the wood, and leaves permanent marks, says Jon Colbasiuc, owner of Supreme Deck Store in Helmetta, Upcoming Jersey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

A wooden deck adds charm to a backyard and serves as the ultimate backdrop for outdoor relaxation, but keeping it in prime condition requires some work. While weather certainly takes a toll, some habits you might practice unwittingly could be accelerating deck rot. We spoke to a couple of deck experts to identify common maintenance missteps, from aggressive pressure washing and harsh chemical cleaners to trapped moisture under potted plants and forgotten debris. By identifying these mistakes and adopting safer maintenance techniques, you can protect your deck from premature decay and preserve it for years to come.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest mistakes homeowners make when it comes to wooden deck care is pressure-washing it too aggressively, which often strips the wood fibers, splinters the wood, and leaves permanent marks, says Jon Colbasiuc, owner of Supreme Deck Store in Helmetta, Upcoming Jersey. When the wood splinters, it opens up recesses where mold can start to grow. This can eventually damage the wood grain, force dirt deeper into the wood’s surface, make it harder to keep the deck clean, and shorten the lifespan of the wood. Instead, Colbasiuc recommends using a soft-bristled brush with deck-specific cleaner, or pressure washing the deck from an adequate distance on a low-pressure water setting.

Another common concern is letting leaves, dirt, dust, pollen, and other debris build up between deck boards, which can trap moisture and eventually lead to mildew or rotting, notes Jake Anderson of Modernize It LLC in Candia, Newly introduced Hampshire. It’s key to regularly sweep the deck with a stiff-bristle brush to keep it clear of such materials. “Regularly cleaning between the boards helps maintain adequate drainage and airflow, especially in the fall when leaves are a more prominent issue,” adds Colbasiuc.

According to recent reports, using a putty knife or special deck gap tool, clean the gaps between deck boards at least twice per season during spring and fall. Even covered decks can have debris that gathers in corners. Trim vegetation that’s within 12 inches of the deck to minimize leaves, berries, and other plant materials from falling onto the deck.

Featuring a telescoping handle and a narrow hook on one end, this tool allows you to clean between deck boards while standing.

It might seem like a good idea to clean a deck with chlorine bleach, but you should avoid using bleach. The cleaner can be very corrosive, which will discolor the wood, and end up destroying the wood’s natural lignin, which can ruin its strength and structure. The bleach also raises the pH of the wood surface, which can make it harder for stains and sealants to work properly in the future. Finally, the bleach can ruin metal objects used on the deck, such as nails, screws, and fasteners. Instead, clean the deck using a nontoxic oxygenated cleaner with an oxalic acid-based wood brightener.

Another common mistake is leaving items out on the deck for long periods of time. “Rugs, planters, and other items sitting against the wood can trap moisture beneath them, which accelerates discoloration and deterioration of the wood,” warns Colbasiuc. This can lead to stains, moss growth, and deck rot. Instead, he recommends choosing breathable rugs specifically meant for outdoor use, elevating a plant container with planter feet, and moving the furniture every so often to help the wood dry between rains.

It has been revealed that you’ll also want to avoid doing anything that can scratch the surface of the wood. A common blunder is sliding around patio furniture with metal legs that can scrape the deck. Either lift the furniture when moving it or add protective pads. “Using metal shovels can scratch wood, create splinters, and scrape away at protective finishes,” says Colbasiuc. “Instead, use plastic-edged shovels, which are a safer option to clear snow from the deck.”.

#55670. Industry News: Our Amicus Brief in the First Circuit $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Case

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (655 w)

Industry News: Our Amicus Brief in the First Circuit $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Case

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Thursday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief in the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, in support of California and other states challenging the Trump Administration's imposition of a $100,000 fee on applications for H-1B visas (which are used by tech firms, research institutions, and other organizations to hire immigrant workers and researchers with various specialized skills).
  • The district court ruling in this case invalidated the $100,000 fee on the grounds that the executive had illegally usurped Congress' power to impose taxes.
  • We are very grateful to Deno Hemonas and Philip Wilkinson of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich Rosati, who worked with me on the brief, pro bono.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Thursday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief in the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, in support of California and other states challenging the Trump Administration's imposition of a $100,000 fee on applications for H-1B visas (which are used by tech firms, research institutions, and other organizations to hire immigrant workers and researchers with various specialized skills).

The district court ruling in this case invalidated the $100,000 fee on the grounds that the executive had illegally usurped Congress' power to impose taxes. It relied heavily on the Supreme Court's recent decision in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the tariff case I helped litigate. A second federal district court later invalidated the fee on other grounds.

We are very grateful to Deno Hemonas and Philip Wilkinson of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich Rosati, who worked with me on the brief, pro bono. Stanford Law School Prof. and former federal judge Michael McConnell, also worked with us on the brief. He is one of the nation's leading experts on executive power, a prominent conservative originalist constitutional law scholar, and was our lead counsel in the Supreme Court phase of the IEEPA tariff case.

Here is a summary of our arguments:.

As the Supreme Court emphasized in its recent decisions striking down Donald Trump's Massive IEEPA tariffs, "the Framers gave Congress alone access to the pockets of the people." Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229, 241 (2026)  The tax power was, as Alexander Hamilton explained, "the most vital of the authorities proposed to be conferred upon the Union." Just months ago, the Supreme Court in Learning Resources applied those fundamental principles to hold that the President may not use a general grant of authority to "regulate … importation" to impose tariffs, because the power to "regulate" is not the power to tax and Congress did not clearly delegate its taxing power. This case asks whether the same President—by imposing a tax of his own devising on the entry of noncitizens and calling it a "restriction" on entry—may accomplish by a different label what Learning Resources forbade.

According to recent reports, the exaction here is a tax. Its "defining feature" is that it raises revenue. Learning Resources, 607 U.S. at 241. It is neither a mere fee contributing to the costs of operating the program nor a penalty. The power to "restrict" entry is not the power to "tax" entry. To limit or qualify entry states nothing about charging for it, and the Government can identify no statute in which the words "restrict" or "restriction" confer tax authority.

Industry observers note that the Immigration and Nationality Act  contains express, detailed provisions for fees and payments, setting each amount and specifying how the funds are collected and spent. This confirms the absence of a generalized, unlimited discretionary presidential taxing power. Congress does not "hide elephants in mouseholes," and this case involves a very large elephant. Whitman v. Am. Trucking Ass'ns, 531 U.S. 457, 468 (2001). In more than a century, no President has used Section 212(f) or Section 215(a) of the INA to raise revenue, a point the Government does not dispute. As the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources, that absence is "strong evidence" the power does not exist.

In a recent development, in addition, the government's interpretation of the relevant statutes violates the major questions doctrine, which requires Congress to speak clearly when delegating power over a major economic or political matter to the executive. The power to impose unlimited taxes on any visa holders or immigrants entering into the United States is undoubtedly a major one. If, nonetheless, the court concludes that Congress did somehow grant the government the sweeping power it claims, it would violate the constitutional nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegations of legislative power to the executive.

I have previously criticized the $100,000 H-1B fee on both legal and policy grounds here, here, and here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that yesterday, the Cato Institute and I filed an amicus brief before the US Court of International Trade, in Gellert Global Corp. v. Trump, the first case challenging Donald Trump's massive 50% Section 338 tariffs against Canadian imports. The plaintiff is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the public interest law firm I worked with on the case challenging the massive tariffs Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). That case resulted in the tariffs' invalidation by the Supreme Court earlier this year.

I previously wrote about the Section 338 tariffs and why they are harmful and illegal in an article in The Dispatch, and a paper for the Montreal Economic Institute.

We are grateful to Daniel Cannistra and others at Crowell & Moring for their invaluable pro bono assistance in helping draft and submit the brief on very short notice. Here is a summary of our key arguments, which should soon be posted at the Cato website:.

This brief explains why Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 cannot be used to impose the tariffs enacted by Defendants, and why doing so violates the major questions and nondelegation doctrines.

The Court should strike down the Section 338 duties for three reasons. First, Section 338 requires that any tariffs imposed be in response to discriminatory trade restrictions enacted by foreign trading partners, and that those tariffs "offset" the barriers imposed by those countries. The Section 338 tariffs imposed by the Trump administration violate both of these requirements. In addition, Section 338 has been superseded by later statutes and is no longer operative.

Recent findings suggest that second, the major questions doctrine forecloses interpreting Section 338 to permit the President to impose extraordinary import taxes whenever another country imposes any trade restrictions or declines to purchase American goods. to "speak clearly" when it assigns to the executive "decisions of vast 'economic and political significance.'" The sweeping power claimed by the administration in this case undeniably raises a major question, and it is at the very least unclear that Section 338 actually grants such vast authority.

Industry observers note that third, stripping the statute's qualitative conditions of operative force violates the nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegation of legislative power to the executive. An extremely high rate ceiling of 50 percent cannot substitute for clear legislative limiting how and when tariffs can be imposed.

Cato and I (together with Prof. Michael McConnell) also recently submitted an amicus brief in litigation challenging Trump's massive Section 301 tariffs.

#55667. Supreme Court Will Review Case Challenging Donald Trump's "Invasion" Executive Order

Supreme Court Will Review Case Challenging Donald Trump's "Invasion" Executive Order

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday, the Supreme Court decided to review Mullin v.
  • Sources indicate that the Trump administration's position on this problem is badly wrong, and has dangerous implications.
  • I also go over the dire implications of adopting a broad definition of invasion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, the Supreme Court decided to review Mullin v. RAICES, a case challenging the legality of Donald Trump's January 2025 "invasion" executive order, which bars virtually all legal migration across the southern border. Trump relies on the Guarantee Clause of Article IV, Section 4 of the Constitution, which states that "The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government, and shall protect each of them against Invasion." The administration claims that illegal migration, drug smuggling, and supposed "public health" risks  qualify as an "invasion" under the Guarantee Clause, thereby authorizing the president to suspend legal migration indefinitely.

Sources indicate that the Trump administration's position on this problem is badly wrong, and has dangerous implications. In my article, "Immigration is Not Invasion" I provide a comprehensive overview of the many reasons why "invasion" - as that term is used in the Constitution and the AEA - must be a military attack, not illegal migration, drug smuggling, or other similar activity. As James Madison put it, "invasion is an operation of war." I provided a shorter overview of the invasion order and its dangerous implications in a 2025 Just Security article.

I also go over the dire implications of adopting a broad definition of invasion. Among other things, it would allow the federal government to suspend the writ of habeas corpus (and thereby detain people - including US citizens - without due process) at any time. It would also give state governments the power to "engage in war" against neighboring foreign countries at virtually any time, even without congressional authorization. And there is much more. This case has major implications that go beyond immigration, and threaten the civil liberties of US citizens, as well as recent migrants.

According to recent reports, the Supreme Court could potentially rule against Trump on statutory grounds, without reaching the matter of the definition of "invasion" in the Constitution. That is what the district court and the DC Circuit did. Alternatively, the Court could rule that the president has purely statutory authority to bar these migrants. But if it rejects these statutory arguments, or at least does so in large part, it will have to reach the "invasion" issue. If the justices do reach that issue, it is vital that the reject the administration's position.

There are also a number of procedural issues in the case (primarily involving the scope of the remedy), which I will not attempt to go over here.

This case should not be confused with the related ongoing litigation over the legality of Trump's invocation of the Alien Enemies Act of 1798. The AEA can only be used to detain and deport migrants when there is a declared war, an "invasion," or a "predatory incursion." There, too, the Trump administration claims illegal migration and drug smuggling qualify as an "invasion," and there too it is wrong to do so (on which see  Part III of my article, my amicus brief in the Fifth Circuit AEA case, which I coauthored on behalf of the Brennan Center, the Cato Institute, and others). As detailed in my article, it is highly likely that "invasion" has the same meaning in the AEA and in the four places where that term is used in the Constitution, enacted just a few years earlier.

I will likely have more to say about this case in future posts and other writings. Stay tuned!

  • Andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents "thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings." Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing "know-your-rights information about U.S.
  • Audai Cote, "the registered agent and individual in charge of I-9 compliance" at the firm, was served with a Notice of Inspection on September 8, 2025.
  • In late September 2025, while the HSI investigation proceeded, both Lattarulo and Cote travelled from Boston to Aruba for a weekend trip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Judge Allison Burroughs (D. Mass.) Friday in Lattarulo v. Mullin:.

Andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents "thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings." Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing "know-your-rights information about U.S. immigration matters," which regularly "amasses hundreds of thousands of views." Georges Cote is currently being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations ("HSI"), the investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security ("DHS"), for employing individuals without a legal right to work in the United States.

Audai Cote, "the registered agent and individual in charge of I-9 compliance" at the firm, was served with a Notice of Inspection on September 8, 2025. Unlike Lattarulo, "Cote is not an immigration attorney—he focuses on personal injury." The firm responded on September 12, 2025, and the government sent Cote a Notice of Suspect Documents on September 25, 2025. The firm was given ten days to attempt to verify the identity and work authorization of the employees named in the Notice of Suspect Documents.

In late September 2025, while the HSI investigation proceeded, both Lattarulo and Cote travelled from Boston to Aruba for a weekend trip. On September 27, 2025, Cote arrived back at Logan Airport from Aruba without problem. Lattarulo made the same journey the following day, September 28, 2025. Lattarulo passed through customs preclearance in Aruba before boarding a flight to Boston.

Sources indicate that when his flight arrived at Logan Airport, three U.S. Customs and Border Protection ("CBP") agents and one HSI officer stopped Lattarulo as he got off the plane. The agents seized his cell phone without a warrant and then downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on the phone. Eight days later, they returned the cell phone via overnight delivery.

Recent findings suggest that the seized cell phone data is right now in a format that is not readable or reviewable, but the government intends to convert the data to an accessible format and search it if the Court permits. The data includes confidential information, including privileged attorney-client communications related to Lattarulo's clients. {The Government was clear that any search of the contents of the phone would utilize a taint team to protect privileged information.} ….

The court held that Lattarulo was likely correct on his claim that the search was unconstitutional retaliation for his speech, and therefore granted "a preliminary injunction enjoining Defendants from accessing the data obtained from the phone before this action is resolved":.

"[T]he law is settled that as a general matter the First Amendment prohibits government officials from subjecting an individual to retaliatory actions, including criminal prosecutions, for speaking out." … The retaliation issue [here] turns on causation—that is, whether the seizure and search of Lattarulo's cell phone would have occurred but for his protected speech.

It has been revealed that respondents have provided no evidence that searches of cell phones are frequently conducted during the kind of employment investigation at matter here, and Lattarulo has directed the Court to sources which suggest otherwise. Indeed, Lattarulo's evidence suggests that any pursuit of criminal charges against employers for employing unauthorized immigrants is exceedingly rare. The fact that the government, after Lattarulo spoke out publicly against it, elected to adopt a highly unusual investigative method that appears designed to inflict a maximal burden on Lattarulo lends substantial support to an inference that its actions were pretextual.

According to recent reports, the stage of the investigation at which the search occurred further bolsters the inference of pretext. Under HSI's own policies, the agency "presumes that employers who, within 10 business days of receiving a Notice of Suspect Documents, verify the identity and/or employment authorization of the listed employees, or take appropriate actions to address the apparent employment of unauthorized workers, have demonstrated reasonable care under the INA." The government's search occurred only three days after Georges Cote first received a Notice of Suspect Documents, meaning that the agency was still early in its period of "presum[ing]" compliance when it occurred. Thus, the government's actions here required it to short-circuit its orderly investigative procedures and cast aside its ten-day presumption of compliance in favor of immediately seizing Lattarulo's phone. That aggressive deviation from protocol strongly suggests that the seizure did not arise from an ordinary investigative motive.

Further, Lattarulo has identified an "otherwise similarly situated individual not engaged in the same sort of protected speech," who was not subjected to the same enforcement action: his law firm partner Audai Cote, who had the same or greater access to the firm's employment records but did not speak publicly about immigrant rights. Indeed, if the government was truly intent on seizing evidence at the first possible opportunity, Mr. Cote, who returned to America a full day before Lattarulo, would have been a more logical target. Nonetheless, the government opted to wait until Lattarulo touched down in Boston the next day and subject only him to an intrusive cell phone search. The balance of the evidence presently before the Court thus suggests that Lattarulo is likely to establish that he would not have been searched except for his protected speech.

{It is true that the presence of probable cause generally precludes a finding of causation in a retaliatory arrest case, but the Supreme Court has recognized a limited exception for situations in which officers who "have probable cause to make arrests [for a particular crime] … typically exercise their discretion not to do so," such as "an individual who has been vocally complaining about police conduct … [before being] arrested for jaywalking," By analogy, the limited record before the Court suggests that searches of cell phones are not regularly conducted during the kind of employment investigation at concern here and that Lattarulo's own law firm partner was not subjected to the same seizure and search of property.}.

Industry observers note that it is true that Defendants can "prevail … by showing that the [search] would have been initiated without respect to retaliation," and here Defendants state that they have additional evidence which would show as much, but they have not provided it because they assert that doing so would prejudice an ongoing investigation…. [T]he Court concludes that the limited record that is before the Court suggests that Lattarulo is likely to succeed on the merits of his First Amendment retaliation claim and that the record before it is therefore adequate to grant the limited preliminary relief contemplated by this order.

Recent findings suggest that the court didn't resolve Lattarulo's Fourth Amendment claim, because it granted the preliminary injunction based on the First Amendment claim. But it did note the following:.

Industry observers note that plaintiffs' Fourth Amendment claim turns largely on the scope of the border search exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement. That exception "is grounded in the government's 'inherent authority to protect, and a paramount interest in protecting, its territorial integrity.'" It allows the government to perform "routine" border searches of electronic devices without suspicion of any crime, and to perform "non-routine" border searches of electronic devices without a warrant, so long as the government has reasonable suspicion. Alasaad v. Mayorkas (1st Cir. 2021).

In a recent development, the question this case raises is: reasonable suspicion of what? In other words, what types of suspected criminal activities can the government use a warrantless advanced border search to investigate? The First Circuit in Alasaad stated that the exception applies to searches for "contraband" or for "evidence of contraband or a border-related crime." Later in its opinion, however, it stated that the exception applies to searches for "contraband, evidence of contraband, or for evidence of activity in violation of the laws enforced or administered by CBP or ICE." In most cases, of course, "border-related crime[s]" and "activity in violation of the laws enforced or administered by CBP or ICE" are synonymous, and the First Circuit in Alasaad appears to have intended to use those terms more or less synonymously.

According to recent reports, the difficulty of this case lies in the fact that the suspected violation at concern—employment of unauthorized aliens in the United States in violation 8 U.S.C § 1324a—involves a law that is "enforced or administered by CBP or ICE" but arguably is not a "border-related crime." Based on the information before the Court, there appears to be no connection between Lattarulo's border crossing (or, more broadly, the government's interest in policing the border) and the suspected crime that formed the basis for the government's border search. Rather, it appears that the government seized on a fortuitous border crossing following a weekend vacation as an opportunity to search for evidence of a domestic crime it was already investigating.

Even though the suspected violation involves aliens and a law administered by ICE, the Court is not convinced that the First Circuit in Alasaad intended for the border exception to apply to investigations into activity that occurred nowhere near the border and that has no relationship to the border crossing during which the search occurred. Nor is the Court convinced that application of the border search exception to this type of investigation would further the principles underlying the exception. Nonetheless, given the novelty of these questions and the fact that a ruling on them is not necessary, the Court will refrain at this point from reaching a firm conclusion on the problem of the border search's applicability….

Sources indicate that mary Lemay and Patrick M. Hanley (Butters Brazilian LLP) represent Lattarulo.

The Best Air Quality Monitors of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Indoor air quality monitors can help you breathe easier at home by detecting hazards you can’t see or smell.
  • Concerned about the dangers of hidden pollutants lingering in the air of typical homes, we decided to test a number of today’s most popular air quality monitors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Indoor air quality monitors can help you breathe easier at home by detecting hazards you can’t see or smell. Gases like radon and carbon monoxide are colorless and odorless but dangerous if inhaled, and these home devices may also identify other pollutants, including volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and airborne particulate matter like dust and pollen. They can serve as a first alert, signaling when to leave an area where the air is unsafe or prompting you to start clearing pollutants and head off health problems. Keep in mind, however, that not all air quality monitors detect all harmful pollutants.

Concerned about the dangers of hidden pollutants lingering in the air of typical homes, we decided to test a number of today’s most popular air quality monitors. We began by extensively researching more than 40 air quality monitors to narrow the field and then selected a range of models to test. (Spoiler: Not all of the air quality monitors we tested earned a spot on this lineup.).

It’s easy to take steps to improve the air quality in your home with an air quality monitor. The best air quality monitor will depend on which pollutants you want to keep track of and whether you prefer a basic or tech-forward model. Our favorite is the Airthings 292 Wave Mini Indoor Air Quality Monitor. It monitors total VOCs (TVOCs), radon, temperature, humidity, mold risk, and outdoor pollen levels. It also comes with smart-home capability and easy-to-use air quality indicators, and it’s suitable for multi-room use.

Ahead, find out what the devices can do and see how the models listed below fared in our hands-on testing to help you choose the best air quality monitor for your home.

Bottom line: Choosing the right air quality monitor depends on specific needs, from detecting VOCs to integrating with smart-home systems.

When it comes to air quality monitors, accuracy is essential. While we didn’t have access to a laboratory for testing, we could offer a measure of control by testing all the monitors under similar situations to see if the readings would correspond when compared to one another. The following monitors all detected the presence of pollutants in our hands-on tests, and we would not hesitate to recommend any of them to help our readers choose a product to detect airborne pollutants in the home.

To measure chemical pollutants in the air without spending a lot, consider the well-priced Wave Mini. The Wave Mini detects TVOCs, humidity, and temperature in the room. After spending a few hours exposed to a dish of oil-based stain in a closed box, the monitor’s TVOC levels spiked. When we compared its temperature and humidity readings to other monitors being tested, the readings were comparable. We believe it accurately portrayed all three readings.

The Wave Mini offers visual indication of air quality in the room, which is accessible when the user waves a hand in front of the monitor. A light flashes green for “healthy,” yellow for “caution,” and red for “poor” air quality.

Industry observers note that people can purchase a hub separately, allowing them to integrate with smart-home products such as Google Assistant and Alexa. The Wave Mini also tracks outdoor pollen levels via the app that syncs with a local weather service. If users don’t have a specific need for monitoring carbon monoxide, radon, or dust, the Wave Mini may be just the right budget-friendly device to keep track of chemical pollutants in the home.

Get the Airthings 292 air quality monitor at Amazon.

According to recent reports, amazon, increasingly offering more of its own brand of products, has entered the air quality monitor field with this device, which measures particulate matter, TVOCs, carbon monoxide, humidity, and temperature. It’s ideal for bedrooms because the small white cube with a little stainless steel vent in front doesn’t have a large display that might keep some folks awake. Instead, a tiny indicator light at the top that shines green, yellow, or red notifies the user of the current air quality. We didn’t find the indicator light to be bright enough to be annoying; it was just bright enough to display the air quality at a glance. However, it only works in a darkened room—it’s not bright enough to see it in sunny daylight.

The Amazon smart air quality monitor syncs with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and we found it simple to connect to both. We were unable, however, to connect the monitor to our Echo Show (not included), although it’s advertised as being able to do so. We’re not sure what caused the glitch, since our Echo Show and the monitor individually synced with the Alexa app, but it’s possible it will only connect with newer models of the Echo Show (ours is an older model). Still, the Alexa app on our smartphone provided excellent real-time readings and charts that made it easy to see the air quality.

In a recent development, we tested this monitor in our test box for VOCs and particulate matter. For the first test, we put a dish of oil-based stain in the box, gave it a couple of hours to infiltrate the air, and then checked the app. The VOC reading had spiked. We then opened the box to check the monitor—the indicator light shone red (hazardous air quality). For the second test, we shook the dust mop over the box and monitored the app on our phone. The PM2.5 reading spiked in about 5 minutes and fell 20 minutes later as the dust settled.

To test the CO sensor, we put the monitor in the garage, started the car, and closed the doors. We watched on our smartphone as the CO reading on the app rose. When we opened the garage door, the indicator light was red. We brought the monitor out into the fresh air, and the light turned green in about 10 minutes.

Compared with the other monitors we tested, the Amazon smart air quality monitor’s temperature and humidity readings were right on target. Overall, we liked this little monitor, and we felt it was accurate and discreet enough not to detract from bedroom or nursery decor.

Get the Amazon air quality monitor at Amazon.

Industry observers note that this monitor was quite an overachiever in our testing! It connects using Bluetooth technology via the Airthings app and provided detailed reports about our home’s air quality. It will also connect to smart-home devices, such as Alexa, but not via Wi-Fi. Instead, users must download the IFTTT app for their smartphone, which allows a connection between Wave Plus and Alexa.

According to recent reports, the first test we performed on the Wave Plus was in a friend’s home where radon was previously detected and is being treated. They have a professional radon detector, so we wanted to see if the Wave Plus would also detect the gas. We positioned it in the basement of the home and left it there for a week.

On our return, we checked the Airthings app and found a radon reading of 3.5pCi/L. This was the exact reading the professional radon detector was showing. When we waved a hand in front of the Wave Plus, it flashed a yellow light that told us the air quality was affected but not hazardous. When we took the Wave Plus outside in the fresh air, the radon level dropped, and the light turned green to indicate healthy air.

Recent findings suggest that we then tested the Wave Plus in our test box where we exposed it for 2 hours to a dish of oil-based stain, a product that contains VOCs. When we checked the monitor, the light was red (indicating hazardous air quality), and on the app we saw that the TVOC reading had spiked. We also compared the monitor’s temperature and humidity readings to those of the other monitors, which were consistent.

We performed one more test—a very unscientific CO2 test. We know that smoke contains CO2, so we took the Wave Plus to the garage and put it on a bench. We used our beehive smoker to blow little puffs of smoke directly on the monitor. The CO2 levels on the app increased slightly, and the indicator light turned yellow. We felt it was detecting some CO2, but we couldn’t tell if it was sensing as much as it should have been. Still, it registered an increase similar to the CO2 detectors on other monitors, so we felt the smoke from the beehive smoker didn’t contain much carbon dioxide.

Get the Airthings 2950 air quality monitor at Amazon or The Home Depot.

It has been revealed that the AirVisual Pro air quality monitor by IQAir boasts advanced laser technology, airflow control, and a crafted calibration algorithm to detect precise particulate matter and CO2 data. We felt the most vital readings on this monitor for allergy sufferers were the PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 readings. These sensors detect various-size airborne particles, ranging from pollen, which is rather large and can be detected by the PM10 sensor, all the way down to ultrafine dust that can’t be seen but is easily inhaled.

The AirVisual Pro syncs with smart-home systems using either Wi-Fi or IFTTT. We tested both, and both worked well. The best thing about this monitor is its large visual display screen. It’s nice to be able to check the app, but in our opinion, it’s even better to see a visual display at a glance without having to use a smartphone first. Another plus: This monitor gathers outside air quality ratings via local weather reports and displays them prominently.

When we put the AirVisual monitor in our test box and shook a dust mop over it, all three PM sensor readings spiked, which indicated that it was detecting a range of particulate matter sizes. After 30 minutes, the PM10 and PM2.5 readings dropped, as we suspected they would, because the dust had settled. However, the PM1 reading only declined slightly, which we think was due to the extra-tiny particulates that remained airborne longer. The PM1 reading didn’t drop for another hour.

Recent findings suggest that the air quality monitor also detectsCO2 levels, temperature, and humidity. We tested the CO2 sensor by putting the monitor in the garage and blowing puffs of smoke on it from our beehive smoker. The CO2 readings increased slightly, but they didn’t spike. Still, that was consistent with our other monitor tests for CO2.

This specific monitor had some trouble with temperature and humidity, as both readings were off by more than 7 degrees Fahrenheit/points compared to the other monitors. Also, it doesn’t detect VOCs. Overall, this is a handy monitor to detect the presence of primary allergy triggers, such as airborne particulates.

Get the IQAir air quality monitor at Amazon or Walmart.

Those looking for a portable air quality monitor to detect pollen and other airborne particulate matter may find the Temtop P600 air quality monitor to be just the ticket. It uses a Quantum Semiconductor International (QSI) laser diode to detect particulate matter as small as 2.5 microns. A highly sensitive diode also found in professional laboratory equipment, it also detects larger particulates, such as pollen, in the 10-micron range.

According to recent reports, the unit has a kickstand that folds out, so owners can stand the monitor on a table, nightstand, or even a tent floor when camping out. The first thing we did was charge it fully using the included USB cord, then we started testing.

Recent findings suggest that there wasn’t too much to test on this one, however, since the P600 detects only airborne particulate matter. We put it in our test box and shook a dust mop over it. This monitor doesn’t sync with smart devices, so we couldn’t monitor the readings remotely from a smartphone. Instead, we checked it every few minutes to see if it had changed. The readings predictably spiked after 10 minutes and then gradually dropped (after about 25 minutes) as the dust settled.

One of the upsides to this Temtop model is that it displays air quality over 12 hours on a chart readout. This helped us see air quality changes over the course of a day. Unfortunately, the battery runs down pretty quickly—we had to charge it every morning for a couple of hours in order for it to run the rest of the day. The alternative is to leave it plugged into the USB cord, but the cord plugs into the bottom of the monitor so it won’t sit upright when plugged in. As a solution, we recommend turning the monitor on periodically to check the air quality in a room and then turning it back off to save battery life.

Get the Temtop P600 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that before we chose monitors for hands-on testing, we researched more than 40 models, looking for various sensor types and paying close attention to buyers’ reviews and ratings. We also reached out to an industry expert to get some additional insight. Lisa Townley, the associate director of product management/replacement parts at Carrier, a global provider of HVAC solutions, states, “As people are focused on the health of their indoor environments more than ever before, it’s imperative that they take steps to improve their living and working spaces, including the air they breathe.” She goes on to say that knowing what’s in your air is notable because you can “take steps to lower the likelihood of mold … better manage allergens and asthma triggers … and create conditions for improved sleep.” She adds that air monitors with advanced technology to detect finer particles down to 2.5 microns or smaller are particularly useful in the home. We took this expert advice into consideration when choosing which products to test.

It has been revealed that for our actual tests—and we must say right off the bat that these were not scientifically controlled trials—we created situations we felt mimicked (or exceeded) real-life air quality problems. To test whether monitors with particulate matter (PM) sensors worked, we put them in a large box and shook a very dirty dust mop over the top. We then monitored the PM readouts on smartphones (or manually) to see when or if they spiked and when they fell (as the dust settled).

We used wood stain, which contains VOCs, including formaldehyde, to test the monitors with VOC sensors. We placed an open dish of oil-based wood stain in the test box and allowed the fumes to infiltrate the box for a couple of hours before checking the readings.

Industry observers note that we got a little more creative when testing other sensors! We tested monitors with carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors by blowing puffs of smoke directly on the monitors using our beehive smoker. We tested for carbon monoxide (CO) by putting the monitors with CO detectors in a closed garage with a car running inside. We tested a single monitor to see if it would detect nitrogen dioxide (NO2) by starting a wood fire in the fireplace of our she shed and then closing the flue and monitoring the readout on our smartphone.

To see how well radon sensors worked, we tested them in the basement of a friend’s home, where we already knew radon was an matter.

Temperature and humidity were casually tested by comparing those numbers with other monitors and using the average of the readings (minus the highest and lowest, which we threw out) to determine consistency.

We looked for readout increases and decreases but didn’t compare actual numbers. The detection numbers varied from monitor to monitor from the start, and we felt that one monitor might receive more exposure to a pollutant than another, even though we tried to keep the exposure levels similar. If the readings more than doubled, we deemed it a “spike.”.

We also examined and analyzed how easy it was to sync the monitors with Bluetooth; Wi-Fi; or If This, Then That (IFTTT) capability.

To arrive at our awards, we gave models points using a rubric—the better we felt the monitor performed during a test, the more points it received. At the end of testing, we added the points and used them to determine the best category for each monitor.

In a recent development, the monitors we tested ranged from single-pollutant sensors, such as simple radon detectors, to multiple-pollutant detection models that tracked the e humidity levels and several toxic gases. In most cases, a consumer will want a monitor that detects the type of air pollution that puts their home and family at the most significant risk.

For example, consumers who live in a region with known radon problems will want to look for a radon detector or a carbon monoxide detector if they’re concerned about automobile exhaust fumes seeping in from an attached garage. In addition, the following factors are important considerations for consumers shopping for an air quality monitor.

Consumer-quality monitors are not as precise as laboratory detectors, but they’re typically good enough to alert household members that airborne particulates and toxic gases are present.

Recent findings suggest that monitors that detect dangerous gases, such as VOCs and carbon monoxide, feature electrochemical sensors that react to the presence of gaseous toxins in the air. In some monitors, these sensors must be manually calibrated, but many of the newer models are precalibrated.

Monitors designed to detect dust, allergens, and other airborne particulates do so by estimating the amount of particulate matter that passes in front of a laser. Though valuable, these measurements may not be exact for two main reasons: larger PM might not drift into the laser chamber, and the laser might overlook the tiniest PM.

Home air quality monitors can detect a range of pollutants and will generally detect one or more of the following. Some may detect additional contaminants, but these are the most common.

While some air quality monitors are relatively straightforward, others are pretty high-tech. For example, some models are Wi-Fi capable, and others connect to smartphones and devices via Bluetooth capability or IFTTT technology. Such monitors come with apps that can be downloaded to a smartphone, and then the app walks consumers through the installation process.

Sources indicate that single-pollutant detectors, such as carbon monoxide detectors, are among the simplest to use because they often just plug into an outlet. If they detect the gas in question, they emit a high-pitched alarm. The best air quality monitor for any individual should be easy to use, depending on the person’s technical skill level. Consumers will want to avoid choosing a complex model with a huge learning curve that requires watching online videos for hours just to figure out how it operates.

Most air quality monitors are relatively small devices, with a sensor unit and a screen that displays how much of the pollutant is presently in the air. It has been revealed that A fireplace should be a source of warmth, comfort, and connection in your home, not a source of worry, claims Chris Maxson, owner and CEO of Acucraft Fireplaces in Major Lake, Minnesota. But it takes some effort and upkeep to ensure your family and home stay safe. If your fireplace hasn’t been cleaned or professionally inspected in years, don’t light a fire until you’ve had it evaluated.

It has been revealed that “Just because a fireplace looks fine on the outside doesn’t mean it’s safe to operate,” warns Maxson. Even when a fireplace sits unused, the chimney can develop obstructions from animal nests, leaves, and other debris. In addition, moisture intrusion, deterioration, and damaged components can create potential safety concerns. Whether you have a traditional wood-burning fireplace or a modern gas fireplace, you’ll want to understand how best to clean and maintain it.

It’s not safe to use a fireplace that has been neglected for an extended period. In general, you should clean a wood-burning fireplace and the chimney once a year before you start using it. Likewise, gas fireplaces need cleaning once a year or as recommended by the manufacturer. Here are the reasons to clean fireplaces, according to Maxson:.

It has been revealed that wood-burning fireplaces produce soot, ash, and creosote as wood burns. Creosote is highly combustible, and accumulated deposits can increase the risk of a chimney fire. Both gas and wood-burning fireplaces also rely on properly functioning venting systems to direct combustion byproducts away from occupied spaces. Obstructions or damaged venting can contribute to dangerous conditions, including carbon monoxide exposure inside homes.

In a recent development, A clean, properly maintained fireplace is more likely to operate as designed. On the other hand, excessive buildup, restricted airflow, and neglected components can interfere with ignition, combustion, and draft.

Cleaning a fireplace isn’t just about making it look good. It’s about making sure the entire system—including the components you can’t see—is functioning properly. Preventive maintenance protects both your home and your investment.

Maxson recommends that homeowners have their fireplace professionally inspected at least once a year, even if they don’t use it very often. “Cleaning removes buildup, while an inspection helps identify hidden issues that cleaning alone won’t solve,” he explains.

For wood-burning fireplaces, annual chimney inspections are essential. “A qualified chimney professional can determine whether sweeping is necessary based on creosote accumulation, soot, debris, and other conditions,” explains Maxson. “Homeowners who burn wood frequently may require additional cleaning during the heating season” for their fireplaces. The firebox also requires routine attention; ash. Remove ash as needed, based on the manufacturer’s instructions, and keep the surrounding area free of combustible debris.

Gas fireplaces should also receive regular professional maintenance according to the manufacturer’s recommendations, typically including an annual inspection. “Servicing may involve cleaning the burner and other components, inspecting the ignition system, and verifying proper operation and venting,” explains Maxson.

Wood-burning fireplaces should routinely be cleaned to manage ash and creosote buildup. A professional chimney sweep can remove accumulated deposits and evaluate the chimney for obstructions, deterioration, or damage. While gas fireplaces burn cleaner than wood-burning fireplaces in terms of ash and creosote production, that doesn’t mean they’re maintenance free, claims Maxson. “Gas fireplaces can accumulate dust, debris, and residue,” he explains. “One of the biggest mistakes gas fireplace owners make is assuming that because there’s no wood or ash to clean up, there’s nothing to maintain.”.

Sources indicate that every home with a fuel-burning fireplace should have working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms installed in appropriate locations. Test them regularly and follow manufacturer recommendations for replacement.

It has been revealed that for wood-burning fireplaces, use properly seasoned, dry firewood. Avoid burning treated lumber, painted wood, household trash, or other materials that can release harmful chemicals or contribute to excessive deposits.

Furniture, rugs, blankets, decorations, and firewood should remain outside the manufacturer’s required clearance areas.

Sources indicate that wood-burning fireplaces can release sparks and embers, while fireplace glass and exposed surfaces can become extremely hot. Proper screens and barriers help reduce the risk of burns and accidental contact.

Ashes and embers can remain hot long after a fire appears to be extinguished. Allow them to cool, place them in a covered metal container, and store that container outdoors on a noncombustible surface away from structures and other combustible materials.

Unusual odors, smoke entering the home, difficulty igniting a gas fireplace, abnormal flame patterns, visible damage, or unexplained soot accumulation are all reasons to stop using the fireplace and have it evaluated. Here come the big boys! The first thing we noticed was how heavy the Wilton heavy-duty bench vise is: an impressive 65.3 pounds, making it the beefiest vise we tested. Be sure to mount it on a sturdy workbench—over a bench leg, if possible, which will help bear its weight.

This large cast-iron vise also firmly held iron rebar as we filed it. The other bench vises we tested can be categorized as either woodworking or shop-type vises, but the Real Avid vise isn’t designed to hold wood or pipes. After successfully testing two shop-type Wilton vises, we were excited to try out the upcoming Wilton Woodworking Vise, especially because it came with pivoting jaw liners designed to grip off-size boards snugly.
